text: Hippolyte Flandrin was the second of three sons, and all three became painters. His older brother Auguste spent most of his life as a professor. Hippolyte showed an interest in the arts from an early age. His most celebrated work, Young Man Seated by the Sea, painted in 1836, is in the Louvre. He painted in the Neoclassical style. He died in 1864.

Over four decades Leslie Ward painted 1,325 portraits that Vanity Fair published regularly under the pseudonyms Spy and Drawl. He produced them as watercolours, and they were turned into chromolithographs for the magazine. They were then usually reproduced on better paper and sold as prints. He was a British portrait artist and caricaturist and was knighted. He lived from 1851 to 1922.

Peter Snayers is known for panoramic battle scenes, depictions of cavalry skirmishes, attacks on villages, coaches and convoys, and hunting scenes. He built his reputation mainly with topographic battle scenes that give a bird's eye view of the battlefield. He also painted large landscapes and portraits of the aristocracy. He often collaborated with other artists. He was a Flemish painter. He lived from 1592 to 1667.

Charles-Joseph Traviès de Villers came from Switzerland and worked in France as a painter, lithographer and caricaturist. His work appeared regularly in Le Charivari and La Caricature. His Panthéon Musical was one of the most famous and widely reproduced musical caricatures of the 19th century. His younger brother Édouard was a painter and illustrator. He lived from 1804 to 1859.

Gustaf Lundberg trained and worked in Paris, and later became court portrait painter in Stockholm. He worked in pastel. His father was a royal chef, and his mother came from a family that included successful artists. He was orphaned at an early age and raised by his grandfather. He was a Swedish rococo artist. He lived from 1695 to 1786.

Mikuláš Galanda grew up in Malá Vieska near Turčianske Teplice. He studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Budapest from 1914 to 1916, and in 1922 he enrolled at the Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague. He painted and illustrated, and became one of the most important pioneers and promoters of Slovak modern art. He is buried in the National Cemetery in Martin.

Francis Danby painted imaginative, dramatic landscapes in the Romantic era, comparable to those of John Martin. He developed his imaginative style as the central figure of a group of artists who have come to be known as the Bristol School. His period of greatest success was in London in the 1820s. He was Irish, born in the south-east of Ireland. He lived from 1793 to 1861.

Rachel Ruysch specialized in flowers, inventing her own style and winning international fame in her lifetime. Her career spanned more than six decades, which makes her the best documented female painter of the Dutch Golden Age. She was born in The Hague and worked as a still-life painter in the Dutch Republic. She lived from 1664 to 1750, and she painted flowers with animals too.

James Northcote grew up in Plymouth and was apprenticed to his father, a watchmaker. In his spare time he drew and painted. Then he left his father's trade and set up as a portrait painter. He became a member of the Royal Academy in 1787, and a member of the Royal Institute of the Netherlands in 1809. He died in 1831.

Portrait commissions, especially of men, made Hubert von Herkomer very successful. Even so, he is mainly remembered for earlier works that took a realistic approach to the conditions of life of the poor. One of them is Hard Times, painted in 1885 and now in the Manchester Art Gallery, which shows the distraught family of a travelling day-labourer. He worked as a pioneering film-director and composer too. Bavarian-born, he became a British painter.

Jacques de Lajoue, a French architectural painter, came from Paris. He became a member of the Academy in 1721. He is noticed for a Perspective that he made for the Library of Saint-Geneviève, and he also designed the title page for the works of the painter Wouwerman. Cochin, Tardieu and other engravers made etchings after him. He died in Paris in 1761.

Albert Baertsoen's subjects were mainly landscapes and especially townscapes, many of his hometown Ghent and, during World War I, of London. His father was an industrialist and textile manufacturer. As a young man he enrolled at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Ghent, studying under Gustave Den Duyts. He was a Belgian painter, pastellist and graphic artist. He lived from 1866 to 1922.

The poets Johannes Jørgensen, Viggo Stuckenberg and Sophus Claussen were close to Albert Gottschalk, in life and in art. He came from Stege on the island of Møn and later moved to Copenhagen. He studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, and then under Peder Severin Krøyer at the Artists' Study Schools. He was a Danish painter. He lived from 1866 to 1906.

Alfred de Dreux, who signed his works that way, came into a privileged and colourful Paris family. He was the first child and only son of the architect Pierre-Anne Dedreux. His real name was Pierre-Alfred Dedreux. He painted portraits and animals and is best known for scenes with horses. He lived from 1810 to 1860, and he died in Paris.

Edward Hicks painted as a folk artist and served as a distinguished Quaker minister. He became a notable Quaker because of his paintings. His birthplace was his grandfather's mansion at Langhorne in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. His parents were Anglican, and his father Isaac was a Loyalist. He painted The Peaceable Kingdom in 1816. He died in 1849.

Knud Baade painted mostly portraits and landscapes, and he was particularly known for his moonlight paintings. Their strong and dramatic contrasts of light and shadow are characteristic of him. He came from Skjold, a village in Rogaland, and was the son of Andreas Baade. He lived from 1808 to 1879. Norwegian.

When Edvard Weie was very young his father left, and the family fell into poverty. To help out, the boy delivered newspapers every morning before school and later worked as a house painter. He came from Copenhagen. He painted as a Danish Modernist and received the Eckersberg Medal in 1925. He died in Frederiksberg in 1943. Dante and Virgil in the underworld is among his early pictures.

Jacob Axel Gillberg's father was a copper engraver serving as an army draftsman when he was born. At ten the boy was already working with the fortification corps. Two years later he was a student at the Royal Institute of Art. Gillberg became a Swedish portrait miniaturist and military officer. He came from Västmanland. He died in Stockholm in 1845.

Alessandro Specchi trained as an architect under Carlo Fontana. He also became an engraver and made a well known series of plates of views of Rome. His parents were Antonio Maria Specchi and Lucrezia Apollonia Frassinelli. He worked in the Italian Baroque and was born in Rome in 1666. He engraved plates for other works too. He died in 1729.

Charles Parrocel specialized in battle and hunt paintings. He studied under his father, Joseph Parrocel, until his father's death, and then with Bon Boullogne became a pupil of Charles de La Fosse. He moved to Italy and attended the Académie de France there as a pensioner. He also engraved. He was born in Paris in 1688 and died in 1752.
